accuracy.evidence: Checked against Development Matters (3 and 4 year olds: make comparisons between objects relating to size, length, weight and capacity), the National Curriculum Year 1 measurement statement (mass/weight: heavy/light, heavier than, lighter than; capacity: full/empty, more than, less than, half, half full) and Common Core K.MD.A.2. Every pair on the balance is physically right (book vs feather, brick vs apple, melon vs cherry, small stone vs big balloon, hammer vs empty box, tin of beans vs sponge, pumpkin vs leaf, banana vs melon), the heavier pan always goes down, and the cup only accepts full at the very top, empty at zero and half full at the middle line.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-measures errors: size confused with mass (the Big but light step puts the bigger-looking thing on the rising pan; feedback 'looks bigger, but its side went up'), reading the balance backwards (first prediction Up vs Down; the lighter step rejects the falling side), nearly full accepted as full (Done at three quarters says 'Nearly! Full means right up to the top'), and a little left called empty (Done at one quarter says 'A little water is still in').

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is direct comparison of mass and capacity: a tilting balance whose beam angle follows which pan holds more mass, a pourable cup in quarter steps with a dashed halfway line and overflow when poured past full, and naming the fill of a jar, bowl or cup. It shares no mechanics with flagsize (lengths and heights lined up from a base line) or flagcount; the 30% shingle gate passed against all flagship labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child puts each thing on a pan and sees its side drop before any rule is stated, discovers in the second step that a big balloon or empty box rises against a small stone or hammer, then has to find the rising side for lighter. Pouring makes them stop exactly at the top, at nothing and at the middle line; the step text confirms the word only after the cup is accepted.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with tempting wrong options: 'The heavier one goes Up' (many children read the raised pan as winning) is disproved when the book pan drops, and 'The big balloon' is heavier than the small stone is disproved when the balloon pan rises and the lab refuses the balloon as heavier with a reason.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions with twelve tagged messages: big means heavy, 'they are the same', up means heavier, both sides loaded, water to the top called empty or half full, a little water called empty or full, book as lighter, 'you cannot tell' (hold them or use a scale), the middle called full, and the middle called empty.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences about a book, a feather, a balloon, a stone and a cup and pass the family limit; canvas text is two to five words with emoji and big tap tiles. Adult text stays under grade 10 and uses the exact terms mass, weight, capacity, direct comparison, balance, heavier than, lighter than, full, empty and half full.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler patterns and the 12% duplicate gate against every lesson, including Big and small, long and short and Grouping materials. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (hefting, the balance, size is not mass, full/empty/half full); adult paragraphs give curriculum goals, how direct comparison works before units, common mistakes and the lab outline.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 dark and 360 px Android light screenshots of all six steps mid-task: both item cards, the tilting beam with the up and down labels, the cup with its top and half marks, the three answer tiles and the Pour in, Pour out and Done buttons all fit at 360 px with nothing clipped; the young class gives large buttons.

accessibility.evidence: walk.cjs: every task completes with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge shows, axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in light and dark themes, no console errors. Every drag has a button route (On, Heavier or Lighter per item, Pour in, Pour out, Done, Full, Half full, Empty) and the canvas aria-label announces each placement, which side went down and the water level.

Department for Education (2013), National Curriculum in England: Mathematics programmes of study, Year 1 Measurement (mass/weight and capacity vocabulary)
Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, K.MD.A.1-2 (describe and directly compare measurable attributes)
